Let me approach this differently. I'll use my chemistry knowledge to analyze the problem:

Terminal alkynes (those with an acetylenic hydrogen) have a C-H bond at the triple bond, which is relatively acidic. This hydrogen can be removed relatively easily (pKa around 25), forming an acetylide ion. This property makes terminal alkynes more reactive in many reactions, particularly nucleophilic additions and substitutions.

Internal alkynes (those without an acetylenic hydrogen) lack this acidic hydrogen. Without the ability to form the acetylide ion, they are less reactive in many reactions that terminal alkynes readily undergo.

The key factor is the presence or absence of the hydrogen atom adjacent to the triple bond. Terminal alkynes with this hydrogen can be deprotonated to form acetylide ions, which are strong nucleophiles and can participate in various reactions. Internal alkynes cannot form these ions.
